evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2024: annual hours U.S. adults spend on health care time and paperwork
evidence_cards.unit: hours per year per adult (mean over adults with a valid answer), or percent of adults
evidence_cards.definition: Edited annual hours adults report spending on their own visits and prescriptions, on others' visits, on medical bills and insurance, and on health care paperwork; plus the share who cared for a friend or family member in the past 30 days. Reported per week, month or year and converted to hours per year.
evidence_cards.method: Weighted mean (ESAQ person weight ESAQWT24F) with a Taylor-linearised standard error from VARSTR and VARPSU; adults who skipped an item are excluded from that item.
evidence_cards.source_locator: MEPS HC-256 (2024 Full-Year Consolidated): EQMVAM53, EQOVAM53, EQMBAM53, EQPPAM53, EQCARE53, ESAQWT24F
comparability: All U.S. adults who answered the questionnaire, not people with Lyme disease or Long COVID: MEPS cannot identify either condition reliably (AHRQ, 2026-09-24).
Fielded in 2024 only: the questionnaire was funded for that year, so there is no trend and no later update.

Self-reported. MEPS top-coded the annual hours at the 99.5th percentile (Table 13 of the HC-256 documentation: 2,080 hours for own visits, 1,040 for others' visits, 720 for bills, 520 for paperwork), so a few very large values are capped. About 6% of respondents skipped each time item, and MEPS notes that about 20% of those who completed the paper version gave no answer to them.
Hours, not dollars. Converting hours to dollars needs a published wage or value-of-time source shown next to the estimate.

scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire document (NCHS Data Brief No. 480 and its companion data tables) reports 2022 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) prevalence estimates of ever/current Long COVID among U.S. adults by sex, age, race/Hispanic origin, family income, and urbanization level. There is no Lyme disease content anywhere in the uploaded material.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a CDC/NCHS government data brief (No. 480, September 2023) reporting how many U.S. adults said they ever had or currently had Long COVID in 2022, based on the National Health Interview Survey. It breaks these percentages down by sex, age group, race and Hispanic origin, family income relative to the poverty level, and urbanization level. It does not report any dollar costs, direct or indirect financial burden, insurance/access barriers, or caregiving burden - it is strictly a self-reported prevalence survey. Long COVID is defined as self-reported symptoms lasting 3+ months after a positive test or doctor's diagnosis of COVID-19, among people who were symptomatic.

contextual_issues: The introduction states Long COVID 'can lead to long-term health and economic impacts on those affected and on society,' citing an external reference (Katz et al. 2023); this document itself does not quantify any such economic impact.

No direct medical costs, direct non-medical costs (travel, paid help), indirect costs (lost income, productivity loss, caregiving time), insurance/access barriers, or diagnostic-delay burden are mentioned or measured anywhere in this data brief.
evidence_gaps: No cost data (direct medical, direct non-medical, or indirect) are present; a cost-of-illness estimate would require linking this prevalence data to a separate cost or claims dataset with a stated price year.
No data on healthcare utilization, treatment-seeking patterns, diagnostic delay, or insurance/access barriers for the people captured in these prevalence estimates.
No longitudinal or duration data beyond the binary 'ever' vs 'currently have' distinction (no information on how long current cases have persisted or their trajectory over time).
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool these 2022 NHIS self-reported 'ever' and 'current' Long COVID prevalence estimates with prevalence estimates from other federal surveys (e.g., Census Household Pulse Survey or other CDC aggregate indicators) that use different survey instruments, question wording, sampling frames, and reference periods (e.g., Aug-Sep 2024 Household Pulse cycles) - these are structurally different measurements, not alternate confidence levels of the same quantity.
'Ever had Long COVID' and 'currently has Long COVID' are overlapping, not additive, categories (current is a subset of ever); they must never be summed.

Subgroup percentages (by sex, age, race/Hispanic origin, income, urbanization) are each separate univariate breakdowns of the same national sample; they are not mutually exclusive partitions that can be cross-multiplied or combined into finer joint subgroup estimates without additional modeling this document does not provide.

sex_gender_findings.finding: Women were more likely than men to ever have Long COVID (8.5% vs. 5.2%) and to currently have Long COVID (4.4% vs. 2.3%) in 2022; the document's footnote indicates these sex differences were statistically significant (p<0.05).

decision_relevance.summary: This document alone supports demographic-pattern analysis (who is more or less likely to report Long COVID) rather than cost modeling, since it contains no dollar figures or cost-related measures. Patients/advocates could use it to see which demographic groups (women, ages 35-49, Hispanic adults, non-metro residents, middle-income families) report higher prevalence. Care delivery teams could use the subgroup breakdowns to prioritize outreach or screening capacity planning by demographic risk pattern. Payers/policy audiences could use the national prevalence rate to estimate the scale of the affected population for program sizing, but would need to pair it with an external, appropriately-dated cost-of-illness source before estimating financial burden, since this document contains no such cost data.
use_cases: A simulator could let users explore how estimated Long COVID 'ever' or 'current' prevalence varies by sex, age group, race/Hispanic origin, income level, or urbanization level, using the document's own 2022 NHIS point estimates and confidence intervals, to understand which populations are more affected - without attaching any cost figure, since none exists in this document.

A simulator could flag for users that population-affected estimates (e.g., applying the 6.9% national 'ever' rate to a population count) are a researcher-added extrapolation beyond what NCHS directly reports, and must be clearly labeled as assumed/projected rather than observed.

package.documentation:
## Source
NCHS Data Brief No. 480 (September 2023), based on the 2022 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS), a federal in-person/telephone survey of the U.S. civilian noninstitutionalized adult population.

## What is modeled
All inputs are 2022 self-reported prevalence percentages for 'ever had Long COVID' (symptoms lasting 3 or more months after a positive COVID-19 test or doctor's diagnosis, among people who had COVID-19 symptoms) or 'currently has Long COVID' (a subset of 'ever'). No dollar costs, healthcare utilization, or caregiving-burden figures appear anywhere in the source, so none are modeled here.

## Subgroup comparisons
The document reports women had higher ever-prevalence (8.5 percent) and current-prevalence (4.4 percent) than men (5.2 percent and 2.3 percent), a difference the source describes as statistically significant. It also reports adults aged 35-49 as the highest age group and adults 65+ as the lowest; Hispanic adults as the highest race/Hispanic-origin group and Asian non-Hispanic adults as the lowest, for ever-prevalence. Input ranges for these paired comparisons were deliberately kept non-overlapping so that simulator sliders and any sensitivity exploration cannot produce a result contradicting the document's own reported ordering.

## Limitations
This data brief does not measure cost, so claims_undercounting and funding-gap limitations do not apply here; there is no cost estimate to undercount or fund. The document also does not present a pooled estimate requiring disaggregation caveats, since all reported figures are already broken out by sex, age, race/Hispanic origin, income, and urbanization. 'Ever had' and 'currently has' are overlapping categories (current is a subset of ever) and must never be summed. Subgroup percentages by sex, age, race/ethnicity, income, and urbanization are separate univariate breakdowns of the same national sample and should not be cross-multiplied into joint subgroup estimates, which this document does not provide. Any attempt to translate these percentages into a number of affected people or a dollar cost is a projection beyond what NCHS directly reports and should be labeled as such.

## Federal cross-check (computed by the system, not by the AI model)

The model only read these quantities from the document; the comparisons below were calculated in code from federal data files. The federal figures are published or surveyed values; the simulator's own outputs are modeled from the uploaded document.

- Percentage of U.S. adults who ever had Long COVID (2022): the document reports 6.9% as the share of all U.S. adults that ever experienced Long COVID; the national survey's 7 wave(s) in that period ranged from 14% to 14.8% (interval bounds 13.4% to 15.4%), so the document's figure is below every survey wave interval in that period. The survey is self-reported adults; a different definition or population in the document makes a gap expected, so treat it as a prompt to check. Federal source: household survey (self-report), 2022-2024; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Percentage of U.S. adults who currently have Long COVID (2022): the document reports 3.4% as the share of all U.S. adults that currently have Long COVID; the national survey's 7 wave(s) in that period ranged from 5.8% to 7.6% (interval bounds 5.5% to 8.1%), so the document's figure is below every survey wave interval in that period. The survey is self-reported adults; a different definition or population in the document makes a gap expected, so treat it as a prompt to check. Federal source: household survey (self-report), 2022-2024; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.

scenarios.goal: Shows how small the sex prevalence gap could be while staying positive.
scenarios.description: Sets women's ever-prevalence to an assumed illustrative low value and men's to an assumed illustrative high value, both within each input's own exploration bounds, to show a lower-bound sex gap that remains positive.

scenarios.label: Wider age gap (illustrative bounds)
scenarios.goal: Shows how much larger the middle-age versus older-age prevalence gap could be.
scenarios.description: Sets the ages 35-49 ever-prevalence to an assumed illustrative high value and the ages 65+ ever-prevalence to an assumed illustrative low value, both within each input's own exploration bounds, to show an upper-bound age gap.

scenarios.label: Wider race/ethnicity gap (illustrative bounds)
scenarios.goal: Shows how much larger the Hispanic versus Asian non-Hispanic prevalence gap could be.
scenarios.description: Sets Hispanic ever-prevalence to an assumed illustrative high value and Asian non-Hispanic ever-prevalence to an assumed illustrative low value, both within each input's own exploration bounds, to show an upper-bound race/ethnicity gap.

scenarios.label: Higher share still symptomatic
scenarios.goal: Tests whether the current-versus-ever ratio rises if both national estimates are higher.
scenarios.description: Sets both national ever- and current-prevalence to assumed illustrative high values within their own exploration bounds to see whether the current share of ever-cases shifts from the default ratio.

scenarios.label: Lower share still symptomatic
scenarios.goal: Tests whether the current-versus-ever ratio falls if both national estimates are lower.
scenarios.description: Sets both national ever- and current-prevalence to assumed illustrative low values within their own exploration bounds to see whether the current share of ever-cases shifts from the default ratio.
